issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette: Karan Mehta was thirty when the mortar strike caught him in the market square. He had been standing with a coil of heavy twine in his hands, watching dust rise in thick, ochre clouds, when a sharp, sudden explosion tore through the air. The concussive blast drove the breath from his lungs. He felt his knees buckle and his body drop into a low, braced crouch, shoulders hunched, arms wrapped tight against his ribs. In that moment, the thick wool of his vest felt impossibly heavy, and the acrid stench of cordite and sun-baked earth filled his nose. What frightened him most was the sheer loss of control, the way the chaos unfolded around him while he remained locked in place, the twine slipping from his fingers. His wife, sitting beside him in the living room years later, would often watch him sit at his own kitchen table and suddenly feel his body return to that exact crouched position, spine stiff, bracing against a blow that had already passed. When Karan returned home, his posture never fully uncoiled. He had come to believe that what had happened in the square was so extreme it seemed to belong to someone else; the story of the blast and the dust felt almost unreal, hard to believe it actually happened to him. His world had shifted. He began to see the environment as a place of latent threat, where danger could materialize without invitation. Nothing in his daily routine felt meaningful anymore, and he questioned whether the steady, deliberate craft that had once defined him was still within his reach. He no longer felt capable of doing the things that had once structured his days, and a quiet resignation settled over his home. Over the weeks and months, Karan found himself constantly on guard. His muscles stayed coiled, his breathing shallow, his eyes tracking the periphery of every room. Ordinary sounds-a car door slamming, a paint can lid popping off, a neighbor's hammer-would make him jump, his body snapping into that same braced position before his mind had time to catch up. His body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger. He worked hard at keeping busy with other things. He spent long hours in his sunlit studio, mixing pigments, priming canvases, and organizing his brushes. The sharp, chemical tang of turpentine and gesso sometimes triggered the old ochre-dust scent, pulling his attention back to the market square. He avoided the evening news, turning away from broadcasts about distant conflicts and urban emergencies, certain that another report about a blast would unravel his composure. He went over and over why the event had fallen to him, why he had been left there standing while others moved on, his thoughts circling the same questions like a wheel on a track. Now at fifty-three, Karan has begun to notice how his capabilities feel distant even within his own studio. A dropped brush or a sudden gust of wind rattling the windows makes him pause, his startle reflex quick, his body on alert. The loss of meaning lingers in his quiet evenings and his solitary meals, even as he continues to paint. His PCL-5 score of 34 maps closely to the steady accumulation of these days. What finally brought him to seek help was a Tuesday afternoon when a passing garbage truck's hydraulic lift threw a loud bang against the pavement. He had dropped his palette knife, his shoulders rising instinctively, and the grief on recall surged up so completely that he sat on the studio floor, waiting for the wave to pass. He is hoping to find a way to let his body unclench, to trust that the world is not always on the verge of collapsing, and to rediscover the steady purpose that once guided his hands.
